newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Red Army headache on road to solution.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Red Army headache on road to solution.

text.p: A Japanese envoy expressed optimism on Monday that Lebanon and Japan would resolve the issue of Japanese Red Army suspects reported held in Beirut that has caused confusion between them for two weeks.
"We are very optimistic that we will reach a satisfactory solution to the matter," Hiroshi Hirabayashi, chief foreign policy adviser for Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, said.
Hirabayashi, who flew to Beirut on Sunday to join efforts to resolve the case, was speaking to reporters after talks with Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.
"We discussed how to proceed on the issue of the Japanese nationals detained here including some Japanese nationals who are believed to belong to the Japanese Red Army," he said.
Hirabayashi was due to meet Lebanese President Elias Hrawi, Foreign Minister Faris Bouez and Prosecutor General Adnan Addoum later on Monday.

The Red Army issue has been mired in confusion since Hashimoto said in Tokyo on February 18 that Lebanese officials had told him they had arrested six Japanese suspected members of the group in Lebanon's eastern Bekaa Valley.
Most Lebanese officials have since been tight-lipped or have made contradictory statements on whether any suspected members of the group are being held.
Asked whether the confusion had negatively affected ties between Japan and Lebanon, Hirabayashi said: "No, to the contrary. I am very optimistic".
However, he declined to identity the suspects.

Asked whether it had been confirmed that some were Japanese Red Army members, Hirabayashi said: "I can't make comments now. We have to identify these people first and both governments are working to get the results in the near future".
Japan and Lebanon do not have an extradition agreement but Hirabayashi said they would study the extradition issue if it was confirmed that the suspects were Japanese members of the Red Army.
"The prime minister of Lebanon and myself agreed to handle this issue in accordance with the relevant laws of both our countries and the international law," he said.
However, an official source in Beirut told Reuters Lebanon was most unlikely to hand over any of the suspects.
"The issue is now in the freezer. It is not probable that Lebanon will hand over any suspects. They will be prosecuted in Lebanon for crimes committed in the country," the source said.
Judicial sources in Beirut said on Friday Lebanese authorities had started interrogating nine or 10 detainees who were mostly Asians and included three Japanese.
Hariri has indicated that Beirut wants to maintain good relations with Tokyo, which pledged at a Friends of Lebanon donors conference in Washington last December to help its postwar reconstruction.
Hariri said a large number of Japanese experts were due to come to Beirut to study projects to which Tokyo could contribute and Hirabayashi indicated that Japan was still on course to help Lebanon.
"We have had very fruitful discussions on how to promote our bilateral relations in terms of the economic and political contexts," Hirabayashi said.
